subject: Astronomy & Space
title: What Is a Supernova?
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: What Is a Supernova?.

hook.text: A supernova is a star's explosive death—briefly outshining an entire galaxy of billions of stars.

buildup.text: When a massive star runs out of fuel, its core collapses in seconds. The rebound blasts the outer layers into space.

discovery.text: Chinese astronomers recorded a 'guest star' in 1054 AD. The remnant is now the Crab Nebula—still expanding today.

twist.text: Supernovae forge elements heavier than iron. The gold in your ring and calcium in your bones were made in exploding stars.

climax.text: Without supernovae, the universe would contain only hydrogen and helium. Every complex element required a stellar explosion.

punchline.text: Stars die so elements can live. You are made of supernova debris.

quiz.question: Why are supernovae essential for life as we know it?
options: They create and scatter heavy elements like carbon, iron, and gold throughout space
They provide the heat needed to keep planets warm enough for life
They clear away cosmic dust that would otherwise block all starlight

details.summary: A supernova is a catastrophic stellar explosion that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy. It occurs when a massive star exhausts its nuclear fuel and its core collapses, or when a white dwarf accumulates enough matter to trigger runaway fusion.
details.whyItMatters: Supernovae are the universe's recycling plants. They forge and distribute elements heavier than iron, trigger the birth of new stars, and their remnants become neutron stars and black holes.
takeaways: A stellar explosion that can briefly outshine a whole galaxy
Created by core collapse or white dwarf thermonuclear detonation
They distribute heavy elements essential for life

faq.question: How often do supernovae happen in our galaxy?
faq.answer: Roughly one to two per century in the Milky Way, though many are hidden by dust. The last one visible to the naked eye from Earth was Kepler's Supernova in 1604. Modern neutrino and gravitational wave detectors would catch the next one even if optically obscured.

faq.question: Could a supernova threaten life on Earth?
faq.answer: A supernova within about 25-50 light-years could damage the ozone layer through gamma rays and cosmic rays. No known massive star that close is about to explode. Betelgeuse, the nearest candidate, is about 650 light-years away — safe by a large margin.
